brief_summary:
Implant-supported prostheses have become a popular treatment option in clinical dentistry because of their long-term clinical success rates and their proven functional, biological, and mechanical advantages.

Dental implants exhibit biomechanical behavior that differs from that of natural teeth because implants lack periodontal ligaments and are in direct contact with bone. Consequently, the occlusal loads received by the implant are transferred directly to the surrounding bone structure. This relationship affects stress distribution within the implant and the peripheral bone and is considered one of the major factors determining implant success. The transfer of stress or energy between the implant and the surrounding bone is influenced by several factors, including the direction of loading and the design and material characteristics of both the implant and the restorative crown.

Soft-tissue attachment around dental implants resembles that around natural teeth, as it includes junctional epithelium and connective tissue fibers. However, some important differences exist. The connective tissue fibers surrounding implants are oriented parallel rather than perpendicular to the implant surface, and the connective tissue around implants is less vascular than that surrounding natural tooth. The formation and maturation of the peri-implant soft-tissue complex require sufficient healing time. Stable soft-tissue attachment is essential for maintaining osseointegration and protecting the underlying peri-implant bone.

Several major factors influence osseointegration, including implant material, implant design, implant surface finish, bone condition, surgical technique, and implant-loading conditions. The first three factors-implant material, macro-design, and micro-surface characteristics-are directly related to the implant itself and may vary according to the manufacturing process.

The macro-design of dental implants may vary considerably, and several aspects of implant geometry can affect treatment outcomes. The implant design should provide adequate primary stability without causing excessive trauma to the osteotomy site, which may result in bone necrosis. It should also contribute to achieving an effective seal at the implant-abutment junction to preserve the integrity of the marginal soft tissues and reduce the risk of mechanical and biological complications. Furthermore, implant design should support the preservation of marginal bone levels during the initial physiological remodeling phase.

Peak horizontal and vertical loading forces are commonly concentrated at the crestal bone level. Therefore, modifications to the implant collar and thread design have been introduced to improve stress distribution and preserve marginal bone. Microthreads at the implant collar, particularly when combined with an internal conical implant-abutment connection, may contribute to improved biomechanical behavior and better maintenance of peri-implant tissues. Surface modifications have also been introduced to enhance osseointegration. These modifications may be achieved chemically by incorporating inorganic or organic components or physically by altering the surface topography at the micrometer or nanometer level.

A dental implant restoration generally consists of three main components: the implant fixture, an abutment that facilitates the support and retention of the restoration, and the final prosthetic restoration. Provisional restorations play an important role in soft-tissue management around implants. A properly finished and polished provisional crown can help establish a healthy peri-implant soft-tissue contour and provide appropriate support for the gingival margin. The decision regarding the timing and type of provisionalization should consider the expected changes in the facial gingival margin and the need to maintain soft-tissue architecture.

Polyetheretherketone is a synthetic thermoplastic polymer characterized by high mechanical performance and has been used as a biomaterial in various medical applications. A modified form of this material, known as BioHPP, has been specifically optimized for dental applications. It is reinforced with ceramic fillers to improve its mechanical properties and make it suitable for the fabrication of crowns and fixed prostheses.

Monolithic zirconia restorations represent another treatment option. These restorations are milled from solid zirconia blocks and may be individually stained to reproduce the appearance of enamel and gingival tissues. Zirconia provides favorable esthetic properties, particularly because it eliminates the dark cervical line that may occur with metal-based restorations. It is also characterized by high strength, durability, wear resistance, and a low risk of chipping or crack formation.

The differences in the elastic modulus, rigidity, and stress-absorbing capacity of PEEK and zirconia may influence the transmission of occlusal forces to dental implants and the surround

brief_summary:
There are many situations where an individual will spend prolonged periods in their bed or chair, often observed in community settings where individuals may have impaired mobility. In many cases, individuals, carers and care providers are not alerted to periods of prolonged immobility. This results in poor self-management and limits access to care support to promote movement. A potential consequence of these prolonged periods of sitting or lying are pressure ulcers, often termed bed sores, which can develop into wounds which are painful and can take a long time to heal. This has a significant impact on the quality of life for the individual affected and is a risk to patient safety and poorer quality of care.

The investigators represent a team of scientists, clinicians, care providers and industry collaborators who have been working with technologies to monitor individuals whilst lying and sitting. Over the last seven years the investingating team have successfully used commercial continuous pressure monitors in community and hospital healthcare settings to evaluate movement patterns over prolonged periods. Through monitoring pressures between the individual and their cushion or mattress they have been able to effectively communicate when they have been less mobile. The technology has also been used to improve the type of cushion or mattress they use to support their health. This has helped individuals understand the risks of being less mobile and supported them to self-manage through regular repositioning and cooperation in care.

The investigators have co-developed improvements to the sensing system and display which is purposefully designed for people living in the community at high risk of pressure ulcers. This was achieved through the principles of co-production, which means working together with patients and the public, service providers and industry partners on a 'fit for purpose solution'. The project has been designed to maximise the input from those who will be using the technology, where innovation must fit around the end user. Through monitoring of posture and mobility we aim to promote self-management through prompts and alerts. Data will also be shared with care service providers, so timely interventions can be made to prevent illness or injury which may otherwise have resulted in hospitalisation. It is necessary to consider the user experiences (UX) of patients, carers and health and social care professionals when exploring the use of medical devices such as continuous pressure monitors. Ergonomic design principles can also reduce the cost of medical device production.

This study will help the investigators determine whether the continuous pressure monitor is acceptable for use in community settings such as the person's own home or a care home. This will mean exploring the views of patients, carers and health and social care professionals who will be using the technology as part of an assessment for the risk of pressure ulcers. The investigator team will work with clinicians to provide training (in person and online videos) and manuals for the use of the continuous pressure monitor and ask nurses to implement the technology in community settings (care homes, nursing home and private homes). This will be used with individuals either at risk of getting a pressure ulcer or who currently have a pressure ulcer. The investigators will then explore how easy the technology was to use and explore any barriers and facilitators for its use in practice. During the study investigators will use interviews, surveys and the data from the continuous pressure monitoring device to assess this. The data will be used to explore how feasible it is to recruit 60 individuals from the community and 20 of their carers and health and social care professionals supporting them. The overall goal of the study is to explore how continuous pressure monitoring can be used at the bedside in the future, which may improve patient outcomes and help design a larger clinical trial to assess the longer-term impact of the technology.
primary_outcomes: Usability of continous pressure monitoring
title: Evaluating Continuous Pressure Monitoring in the Community

brief_summary:
The goal of this clinical trial was to compare two methods of pain control in adults having breast-conserving surgery. The study compared a chest wall nerve block called a PECS II block with lidocaine given through a vein during surgery.

The main question it aimed to answer was:

• Does a PECS II block lower the amount of opioid pain medicine needed during the first 12 hours after surgery compared with intravenous lidocaine? The study also looked at pain scores after surgery and the amount of remifentanil needed during surgery.

Researchers compared participants who received a PECS II block before surgery with participants who received intravenous lidocaine during surgery.

Participants:

* Received either a PECS II block before surgery or intravenous lidocaine during surgery
* Had their pain scores and pain medicine use recorded for up to 12 hours after surgery
primary_outcomes: Postoperative tramadol consumption
title: PECS II Block Versus Intravenous Lidocaine for Analgesia in Breast Surgery

brief_summary:
The goal of this clinical trial is to learn whether daily use of GROPLUS, an energy-dense milk powder, can improve growth in Indonesian children aged 24 to 48 months who are underweight. The main question it aims to answer is:

\- Does taking Investigational Product (milk-product) for 6 months improve children's weight relative to their age?

Researchers will also assess changes in height, weight relative to height, body mass index, head size, growth rate, digestive comfort, and safety during the study.

Participants will:

* Complete a 7-day feeding trial to check whether they can tolerate and accept the study product.
* Drink two servings of Investigational product (milk-product) each day for 6 months.
* Visit the study site regularly for growth measurements and other assessments.
* Have their digestive symptoms, product use, and any health problems monitored during the study.

The study will enroll at least 74 children. All participants will receive GROPLUS, and there is no placebo or comparison group.
primary_outcomes: Change in Weight-for-Age Z-score from Baseline to Month 6
title: Nutritional Status Evaluation in Underweight Indonesian Children Receiving 0.89 kcal/mL Milk Powder - Site Makassar

brief_summary: Approximately 20-30% of patients with schizophrenia show poor response to standard antipsychotic medications, which is defined as treatment- resistant schizophrenia (TRS), yet the underlying pathological mechanisms remain largely unknown. Brain organoids, also referred to as cerebral organoids, have emerged as a promising tool for modeling neurodevelopmental disorders in the laboratory. In this observational study, blood samples will be collected from TRS patients and their family members to generate personalized brain organoids. This study aims to elucidate the mechanisms of TRS and to provide preclinical evidence for developing personalized intervention strategies.
primary_outcomes: Association Between Organoid-derived Biological Characteristics and Clinical Phenotypes
title: Mechanisms and Interventions of Treatment-Resistant Schizophrenia Based on Brain Organoids
